name: Name
body: Over the years, Orsus had grown accustomed to the idea that he would sometimes behave unexpectedly, unpredictably. Even these events tended to follow a familiar pattern, however—a red mist descending, and when next he came to his senses, he was standing alone in an ocean of blood and bodies. Taking the child had not been the mission. He had been sent to slay Vlad Tzepesci's heir, not return with him, especially after losing three warjacks and most of his troops in the process. Orsus knew enough of the Orgoth to know that they had little patience for disobedience, for failure, and that their reprimands were swift and severe. Another man might not have returned at all, but Orsus had left fear behind him long ago. What drove him now was similar to the impulse that had spurred him to trigger the trap back in the clearing: He was fascinated rather than disturbed by the unexpectedness of his own actions, and he wanted to see where they would take him. What had stayed his hand? He had slain children before, when the red rage came over him, and theirs had always been the deaths that haunted him the most. He had never killed a child in cold blood, however. When the Orgoth sent him on this mission, he had wondered if he had changed enough as a man to do so now—and it turned out that he hadn’t. The child’s courage had surprised and impressed him, and that was part of it. He was reminded of the boy in his memory, large and strong but terrified, as he tried to stand between the Tharn and his family. Had that boy been himself? He no longer knew, and it didn’t matter. That had been part of it, but not all.

name: Name
body:
Another memory was there, too. Not as clear as the one of the fire and the cellar, the blood and the monsters, but no less red, no less haunting.
That memory was filled with shadows, lit by flickering tongues of fire. This one took place in daylight that was too bright, too clear, too sharp. It hurt his eyes, seemed to pierce his brain.
He was fighting monsters again. Demons. Nightmares. Intrusions from another place, things that had no business being in this world at all. He was fighting to defend the empress, and, in the fragmented landscape of his memories, she was betraying him at the same time, chaining the howling axe to his wrist and banishing him into the wilderness.
In the memory, though, that hadn’t happened yet. He was fighting until there was nothing left of him. The axe he carried then—he had named it Lola, though he couldn’t and wouldn’t allow himself to remember why—was reduced to little more than splinters of metal in his hand. His face and chest were bathed in blood and ichor, traced with wounds both large and small.

name: Name
body:
Yet, he wasn’t fighting just to protect the empress. He was fighting for something else. A girl child. Who was she? Her hair was spun gold in that too-bright sun, her eyes pleading as they met his, and so familiar.
Pleading because she was hurt. She was dying. Why was she here? They had brought her here to make him fight—as if he had ever balked at fighting for them. They had brought her here, and now she was dying because of him.
He felt the fight drain out of him, a feeling he had experienced only once before in his life, when that bone knife had pierced his innards and he had known he was dead. He was dead again at that moment, though not from any injury. This wound pierced his heart, his mind. She was dying because of him. He couldn’t save her. He hadn’t saved his mother or his sister. He hadn’t saved Lola. Now he couldn’t save her.
He couldn’t save anyone.
He collapsed to his knees and gathered the little body into his arms. She was dying, and she reached up a hand to touch his cheek, her handprint a mark of blood that he could feel as it cooled on his skin.

name: Name
body: Who was she? Branka, they said that was her name. They said she was his daughter. More than that, they said she was Lola’s daughter. And yet she was gone. Gone again. And with her went some part of him, his memories shattering into blood and pain until he was in the vaults beneath the Greylord stronghold, where the empress he had sworn to serve clamped this curse to his hand. Days, months, years of madness followed, until that bloody beach, until the Orgoth gave him new purpose. The memory of Branka—was it real? Had it ever been? It didn’t matter. He had seen her eyes, pleading but not broken, even as she died. Whether it was real or not, it was there, inside him, a splinter working its way through him. Her eyes had been like the boy’s, when he stood in front of Orsus’s axe and demanded that he spare the life of the warcaster—or kill him to get to her. At the end of that battle, if it had ever really happened at all, Orsus had carried Branka’s small, broken body into the woods to bury her. It was there that the soldiers of the Motherland had fallen on him, eventually dragging him back to his fate. When he spared the boy, when he gathered him into the arm that wasn’t shackled to the demonic axe, he hadn’t been picking up the heir of Vlad Tzepesci at all. He had been gathering up Branka’s corpse once again.

name: Name
body: Did it matter if it was real? It proved something to him. Whatever else he was, whatever else he had ever been, once upon a time, he had known love. He had fought for something that was worth fighting for. He had been something more than a weapon. He had accepted this mission, he realized, partly to test himself, to see if he still was something more a weapon. When he arrived back at the lands the Orgoth had taken with the child he was supposed to murder on the saddle before him, he supposed he would find out. *** Sorscha dreamed of fire and blood. She dreamed of a battle against the Butcher, though not the one she had just fought and lost to. Cities burned as armies hundreds strong clashed, machines and monsters throwing themselves against other machines and monsters, rendered to scrap and bits of blood and bone. She and the Butcher stood above it all, somehow, so that it spread like a panorama on all sides of them. The smoke from the fires filled her lungs, the heat puckered her skin, the cacophony of battle became the sound of her own rushing blood and beating heart.

name: Name
body:
The Butcher was before her, but his face was wrong. It wasn’t his face now; it was her father’s face, it was Vlad’s face, it was the face of one of the officers who had trained her at the Druzhina. The Butcher, with his hateful, shifting face, stood in the fire, embers raining down around him, that monstrous axe still clutched in his right hand.
He wasn’t fighting her. She could kill him with Frostfang. One blow could destroy that changing face forever, but as he stood there, arms at his sides, awaiting the killing blow, she found the anger, the rage, the hurt all draining out of her. There was no satisfaction to be had from killing him now.
The Butcher’s face became that of a little girl. Someone Sorscha didn’t know but recognized immediately. And as recognition dawned, the dream changed.
First, the sounds of the battle were replaced with the notes of songbirds. Then the flames congealed until there was only one fire, contained in the hearth of a cabin. The stench of smoke and blood became the scent of chamomile flowers, the darkness of the battlefield the golden light of the late afternoon sun.

name: Name
body:
On the floor before the hearth were two children. One of them she recognized now as Vlad’s son, the one whose safety was entrusted to her and whom she lost to the arms of the Butcher. The other was the little girl whose face she had just seen in the Butcher’s own. She walked toward them. She wanted to say something—to ask how they got here, how they were, whether they were okay—but her lips felt as if they were sealed shut.
The two children rose as she approached, and they reached out their small hands to take hers. They both looked up at her expectantly. What did they want?
***

name: Name
body:
Sorscha awoke to a monstrous skull leering down at her, and her first thought was that she was dead and had been dragged into some kind of hell by the Orgoth. The pain that was unraveling every part of her body and driving a huge, rusty spike directly through her brain seemed to support this interpretation.
The thing that leaned over her didn’t look much like the Orgoth, though, or like the nightmares she had fought during the Infernal Wars years ago. It more closely resembled the monsters that Bhodan Lesnoi had conjured from the woods. When it spoke, it did so in halting, heavily accented Khadoran, its hesitation less that of someone who didn’t know the language well than of someone who was unaccustomed to speaking much at all.
"Ve veren’t able to save ze eye," it said to her, "but ve kept vhat vas left for you—a souvenir." Only when the figure laughed did Sorscha fully realize that the skull wasn’t actually its face at all but just something it was wearing. It was a woman, daubed in some kind of natural paint, her long white hair braided beneath the deer skull that served her as a headdress.

name: Name
body:
The nails on her hands had grown out into talons; now and then, Sorscha could feel them raking lightly across her body as the old woman applied poultices and unguents or whatever it was she was doing.
"What…eye?" Sorscha managed to croak out, the effort of doing so making her throat feel like she had coughed up razors.
The crone just laughed again. "You are avake now," she said. "Strong one. Not for long, zhough, I fink."
Sorscha struggled to say something else, tried to lift her arm. It was like trying to lift a warjack with her bare hands. Even the effort of the attempt was too much, sending spikes of pain through her head that caused her vision to swim with bright lights.
"You vill rest again now," the old woman was saying, but her voice seemed to be receding, as though she were sinking farther and farther away. "But you vill heal, and soon you vill be strong again. Ve shall make it so."
Even as the crone’s laughter seemed to retreat so too did the sight of her, as if Sorscha were slowly falling down a very long, very deep tunnel until there was only darkness and silence and, eventually, even the pain faded away.

name: Name
body:
***
"—my fault," a voice was saying next to her bedside. She heard it first, in the dark, before she was able to force an eye open to see her surroundings. This wasn’t the old woman’s voice; it was a man’s voice, familiar. "There are times," the voice said, "when I don’t know what I’m doing anymore. When I feel that I’ve let everyone who matters down."
She recognized the voice as Omirov’s, but she didn’t recognize her surroundings, not right away. She was in some kind of hard bed, looking upward at a natural cave ceiling where, here and there, tree roots dangled through. The light of her surroundings was dim but warm, likely cast by lanterns or candles.
Omirov was apparently sitting by her bedside, on her left, though she couldn’t see him without turning her head. Obviously, he didn’t know she could hear him. He was talking as much to himself as to her as if she were a priest, hearing his confession.
"Vlad entrusted me with all of Umbrey," he said, "so it would be here for his son. Yet, I let it be taken from me. You entrusted me with the young prince for only a day, and I lost him. The witches say that when the Tzepesci line is broken, Khador is doomed. Have I broken it? Have I doomed us?"

name: Name
body: With immense effort, Sorscha found that she was able to lift her left hand, to reach out toward his voice, and to let it fall on Omirov’s arm. She felt him start, confirming her suspicion that he hadn’t expected her to be awake. "You… didn’t lose Umbrey," she managed to say, her throat dry, scratchy, but much less painful now. "This… is Umbrey. Umbrey is here." "Sorscha," Omirov said, taking her hand from his arm and squeezing it gently in his own, "you shouldn’t talk." She tried to shake her head but only partly succeeded, the pain of even that minor movement filling her vision with stars. "No time… to coddle me," she said. "If Vlad… is lost… we both lost him. But… the Butcher… didn’t kill. Took him." "She’s right," another voice said from the other side of the cave-like chamber. This one she recognized, too, smooth and charming. Bhodan Lesnoi. "The boy lives. The Orgoth must have some plan for him." "Then we have to rescue him," Omirov said, standing abruptly. Sorcha felt the pull in her left arm as he rose.

name: Name
body:
"I’m… coming, too," she said, trying to sit up even as the room swam around her.
"You’re injured," Omirov said.
"Have to." Sorscha waited for the room to stop spinning, for her vision to focus, and by the time it did, Bhodan Lesnoi was standing beside her, his hand on her right shoulder.
"And so you shall," he said, "but not yet. We will prepare an escort to accompany you. It will take time for us to be ready to travel, so, until then, you rest. Heal. You have my word that we will not leave without you."
"That’s good," Sorscha said, collapsing back onto her bed. "Good enough."
***
By the time Sorscha next awoke, she was still certainly not recovered to one hundred percent but felt closer than she probably should have been, given the extent of her injuries. Though she still felt a bit shaky, she found that she could sit up, and the room stayed still around her.
For the first time, she truly took in her surroundings. The chamber was relatively small, lit by candles tucked into small divots carved from the cave walls, and beside her were two simple stools where her earlier visitors had likely sat.

name: Name
body:
She was no longer wearing her warcaster armor and had, indeed, been stripped down to only her underclothes. Daubs of paint or dirt had dried on her skin here and there, but her flesh was remarkably unscarred, unbruised.
The bed on which she now sat was little more than a cot, and she found that she could swing her legs off it and even stand, albeit shakily. At the far end of the small chamber, a table had been placed, upon which were several earthenware vessels containing different colored pastes. There was also a glass jar, its lid screwed tight, in which a jellied blob floated in a clear liquid. A small mirror had been left atop the table, and in it she could see her reflection.
Though most of her bruises were gone, there were still some on her face, and a bandage wrapped around her head at an angle, covering her left eye. Or… no… she reached up her hand, gently, and touched first her cheek, then the bandage itself, feeling the concavity beneath. The words of the old woman came back to her, and she picked up the glass jar, turning it until its contents—though still too smashed to really be recognizable—at least became more obvious.

name: Name
body:
"We did what we could," Lesnoi’s voice said from the chamber doorway behind her.
"It was more than I could have expected," she replied. "How long has it been?"
"Less than two days," he said. "When the spirit is willing, we have ways of mending the body quickly."
"And my spirit was willing?" she replied with a rueful chuckle. "That’s a surprise."
"I think you have reasons of your own," he said. "It is not for me to say what they are. How do you feel?"
"All things considered? Like a million Talons. I think I should be dead."
"You might have been," he agreed. "Under other circumstances. Do you feel well enough to walk?"
"I could use a drink," she said and then caught herself. "But don’t get me one. I think I can walk."
She still held the glass jar in her hand, and considered keeping it—a souvenir, as the old woman had said—but she sat it down on the table, instead. "I don’t need it anymore," she said quietly.
"If you are up to it," Lesnoi said, "you’ll find your clothes in the next chamber. I’ll be waiting outside. Call out if you need me, but I don’t think you will. Once you’re ready, there’s something I think you should see."

name: Name
body: Outside, the sun was shining, and the air was sharp with cold. Stepping out into it made Sorscha ache in places she hadn’t even known were hurt and sent a sharp, keening pain through the place where her eye had been. She blinked—was it winked now, she wondered—against the sunlight as she walked where Lesnoi was standing. He wasn’t what she was looking at, though. A Khadoran ’jack stood in the middle of the old road. An older model, not one of the shiny new ones that the Winter Korps utilized. In each of its hands, it held a massive mechanikal axe, and it was heaving as though it strained against some invisible leash. Its head was pointed toward the west, and it occasionally jerked from side to side like a hunting hound scenting the air. "Drago," Sorscha said softly, recognizing the old warjack that had fought so often at Vlad’s side. "It arrived while you were unconscious," Lesnoi said. "It came to us unaccompanied, just as it is. At first, we thought we would have to array defenses against it, but it had no interest in us. It seemed to be looking for something. It has been here ever since, just like this. It seems that it wants to go somewhere, but it’s waiting for something. We have assumed it’s waiting for you."

name: Name
body:
Sorscha walked slowly toward the familiar hulk. She could feel its cortex; it was wide open to her. She had felt personalities in old warjacks before but seldom as strong as this. It wanted to go west. It was as if it somehow knew that the young prince was in danger, and it had come to rescue him. It felt less like it had come to help her than like it was waiting for her because it needed <I>her>/I> help. Less like it was following her than she was following it.
When she linked her consciousness to Drago’s, she could feel its rage. She had seen things like this before. Warjacks that were closely bonded to their warcasters would sometimes continue fighting in their defense, even when the warcaster fell. But Vlad had fallen long ago, and to see the warjack somehow transfer that bond to his son…
"It’s here to help," she said, laying her hand on the heaving metal side of the massive warjack. "And we’ll need all the help we can get."
***
North of Uld Vroggen, Orsus was met by a small expeditionary force sent to intercept him and take him west rather than back to Ohk. How they had known he was coming or where to find him he wasn’t sure, but he had quickly learned that the Orgoth had their ways. If they were surprised to see his young passenger, they didn’t show it.

name: Name
body:
The force was even smaller than the one he had taken to Old Korska, and it didn’t slow his travel time at all. They moved mostly at night, despite the biting cold, because they were traveling through parts of Khador that hadn’t yet fallen to the Orgoth. They met no resistance along the way, however, as most Khadoran forces had been pulled back to cities and forts in preparation for expected Orgoth strikes. Indeed, most of the inhabitants of this land had already fled the countryside for the putative safety of city walls.
Rather than north to Ohk, they traveled south and west into the volozk of Razokov. The lands here grew hilly as opposed to the rolling and snow-covered plains they had left behind, and soon Orsus was able to deduce their destination. He thought he had been there before, but he could no longer remember when or why.
Razokov had been one of the easiest Khadoran territories for the Orgoth to conquer because there was very little within the volozk. Ragged, hilly shoreline that ran from the Lothpool delta toward Ohk, with no major cities and only a single notable fortification. Much of the land here was desolate, but this place had once been the seat of a kingdom in ancient times, and the palace of that kingdom was their destination.

name: Name
body:
The people of his former homeland called it Khazomir’s Palace, named for the ruler of that lost fiefdom, which had been sacked by the Kossites centuries before. What Orsus remembered of the ruin was that it was rumored to be haunted, no less than the nearby Vescheneg Headlands, which were supposedly cursed by a giant long ago. The Orgoth explored these regions on their last visit here, and some of their deathless remnants were rumored to still exist in catacombs beneath the desolate hills.
When Orsus had last seen the ruins—if the memory really belonged to him at all—they had been little more than a forlorn pile of stones. For those with imagination, it was possible to see the grandeur that the structure might once have possessed, but it was also easy to pass by without even paying them much notice, especially with the lingering smoke that hung over the hillsides from volcanic activity in the nearby headlands.
The Orgoth had transformed the ruins with the grim industry for which they were known. Warjacks and soldiers milled around outside the palace itself as he approached, parting to let him pass. Pits had been dug nearer to the ruins, where the Orgoth performed sacrifices to their Felgoeth masters. Smoke rose from some of these, mixing with the smoke that clung to the hills. The faint sulfur smell of the volcanic ash mingled with an uncomfortably appetizing scent of burnt meat.

name: Name
body:
Though the child in his saddle had been frightened the entire trip, this was the first time since the battlefield that he had displayed visible fear as he looked around at the Orgoth forces, at the sacrificial pits. Orsus could feel a shiver pass through his small body. Perhaps, in times past, he would have attempted some sort of comforting platitude. Now, he rode in silence.
A trio of warwitches met him on the steps of the palace.
"The Night Scourge awaits you inside," one of them said, her voice seeming to slide into his mind rather than issue the words from her lips. She made no mention of his cargo.
Orsus wrapped his free arm once again around his diminutive captive and dismounted, following the three witches into the remains of the great palace. Farther inside, the ruin was better preserved than it appeared from without, and there were still some chambers intact. While it was day outside, the smoke and clouds made the interior of the palace nearly as dark as a tomb, and he passed sculptures and bas reliefs, their features rendered sinister by age and the flickering light of torches and fires.

name: Name
body:
The witches led him through the ruins, moving deftly and silently. Outside, there had been soldiers in multitudes. Within the palace, Orsus saw no one except his guides, who moved like ghosts.
Though a surprising amount of the palace was still intact, time and neglect had worked to erase much of its original dimensions and purposes. The chamber into which he was eventually led might once have been a throne room or a cathedral, with a wide dais set atop a short series of broad steps. Behind the dais were several columns broken off at various heights, and the ceiling of the chamber was gone entirely, leaving it open to the sky.
From here, one of the three moons of Caen was visible even in the daytime sky, a smudged crescent partly obscured by clouds and smoke. It hung above the broken pillars, where a stained-glass window might once have been. It seemed to be part of the room’s decoration, and Orsus could almost believe it wouldn’t move from its spot unless and until Hellaine gave it leave.

name: Name
body:
That was who waited for him atop the dais. Sabbreth once more stood to her side, but no one else was visible, save the three warwitches who led him, and Orsus noted that few other souls would ever have dared to meet him without reinforcements, even when he was ostensibly under their command.
"Orsus," Hellaine said by way of greeting, that deadly smile again on her lips. "They whisper to me that you are mad. Perhaps they are right—one must, perhaps, be either mad or foolish or very, very brave to return alone without having accomplished one’s mission."
Orsus said nothing in response, standing with the child still in his free arm, the axe hanging at his side, its many voices silent for now.
"Do you expect a reprimand?" Hellaine asked. "I imagine this is what you would have gotten from those you served under in the armies of your so-called homeland. Yet you must know that our reprimands are seldom anything you would survive. Still, here you are. Would it surprise you to know that we have no such intention? Indeed, we have a reward for your service."

name: Name
body: This did surprise Orsus, even if it were merely a ruse to build up hope, only to dash it. He could read nothing from this woman, and he wouldn’t rise to the bait. "The heir dead is adequate to our needs," she continued. "The heir at our mercy? Better still. Without even knowing, you have served us admirably—perhaps that is your gift. Our punishments are harsh, as you well know, but our rewards…" With that, she stepped to one side. Standing behind her was a child dressed in black. No older than the boy Orsus held in his arms. Her hair was as dark as her clothes, but Orsus recognized her eyes, knew them even before the warwitch spoke. "Branka, come say hello to your father." ***

name: Name
body:
Even this far south, the wind of a Khadoran winter was cold and sharp. It stung her face, chapped her lips, burned in the place where her left eye had been. Ahead of her, Drago trudged through the snow, steam pouring off its blazing boilers, its head down like a hunting hound that has scented prey.
"Horses are in short supply these days," Omirov had told her, but he had managed to scare one up for her nonetheless: a gray mare named Roan, who moved at a steady pace, despite the deep snow.
When it was still a kingdom, Umbrey had been the domain of horse lords, and that tradition of armed cavalry wasn’t gone, even though there weren’t as many horses available. Instead, the former liegemen had tamed massive bears pulled from the wilderness by the druids—and Omirov assured her that "tamed" here was a generous term.
A unit of these unusual cavalry moved at a surprisingly quick gait through the snow behind her, their riders armed with stubby, wide-barreled blunderbusses. Around them were arrayed the rest of her force, made up almost entirely of liegemen selected by Omirov for the mission—the name itself a misnomer, as their numbers were comprised of almost as many women as men.

name: Name
body:
There were hunters carrying long rifles and wardens with heavy axes and decorated shields. Their demeanor was unusual, a combination of woodcraft and military discipline that Sorscha found surprisingly easy to command, despite its unfamiliarity. Among the liegemen were soldiers called primalists who were gifted in the arts of the druids, who had been trained by shamans in the old ways, and who could command magic to assist their fellows.
Bhodan Lesnoi and his beasts accompanied her as well, but they stayed at a distance, keeping to the woods and the furrows. Sometimes they could be seen loping along at the edges of her vision like shadows. Other times, the only indication of their presence was the ravens that swooped overhead.
It had been Lesnoi’s ravens that reported where the Butcher had taken the boy, and it was Lesnoi who told her that, while the Umbrean troops and monsters would accompany her, it would be she who would have to venture into the ruins to find him and bring him out, according to the auguries that had been cast. This suited her fine.

name: Name
body: Omirov had wanted to come with her too, but she had talked him out of it. "I don’t know what I’m walking into here," Sorscha said. "None of us do. There’s a real chance this doesn’t work. And if it doesn’t work, I need someone I can trust to make the next attempt. Vlad trusted that to you. Now it’s my turn." "This had better work," Omirov said, putting his hand on her shoulder with a sad smile, "or I’m never going to forgive you." The remaining Winter Korps forces who had accompanied her had also been left behind in Old Korska. A few had come and volunteered to follow her on this new mission, which surprised her. She didn’t think she had ever shown them anything that would engender that sort of allegiance. She had given them platitudes, similar to what she had handed Omirov, though less true, telling them that she needed eyes and ears that she could trust. The fact was, she had already put them through more of a ringer than they deserved; she couldn’t bear the idea of feeding what was left into a meat grinder from which they probably would never return.

name: Name
body:
"Bring him back" was the last thing Omirov had said to her, and she knew it was a plea, not an order. She had said she would, but as she rode through the biting cold, she wondered if she really intended to.
"When the spirit is willing," Lesnoi had said. What was her spirit willing to do? Had she really allowed herself to be pulled back from the brink of death to save a boy she barely knew, the son of the lover who had left her behind? Had his sacrifice on her behalf reminded her enough of his father to rekindle something like love in her frozen heart?
It hadn’t been the young prince she dreamed of, as she lay on death’s doorstep. It hadn’t even been Vlad. The boy was still alive, but so was his captor. Her fight against the Butcher hadn’t gone the way she had hoped, but she had survived it, which meant there was another chance.
She had dreamed of fire and blood and the Butcher of Khardov at her mercy. Maybe that dream could still come true.
***
Orsus Zoktavir sat on broken steps outside the palace of Khazomir, his head bowed. Was he crying? No tears were falling from his eyes, no sobs wracked his massive frame, yet even he couldn’t tell for sure. All he could feel was the weight of the axe chained to his hand, the aching hollow in his chest and stomach.

name: Name
body: Orsus Zoktavir knelt in the snow and dug a makeshift grave with the haft of a broken axe named for the woman he loved. The ground was hard and frozen, and when the axe could no longer effectively dig it out, he used his fingers, gouging at the dirt until they were bloody. He couldn’t feel the pain, but he saw the blood. It seemed that his hands were always covered in blood. Into the hole, he put the bundle that he carried. What was in the bundle? He couldn’t think about that. Couldn’t picture those eyes, so much like Lola’s. Couldn’t remember that, for a brief moment, he had held a part of Lola come back to him. Had held something they had made together, something good that was wrenched, somehow, from all this death and pain. Now it was gone again, and he put it into the hole. Orsus Zoktavir stood in a chamber deep underground as the woman he had sworn to serve fastened damnation to his wrist. His fingers clamped around the handle as the voices filled his mind, screaming that he had killed them. He probably had.

name: Name
body: Orsus Zoktavir waded in bloody sand on a beach littered with corpses. His thoughts were somehow both empty and filled with screeching, the sound of an engine tearing itself apart. It was the woman who cut through it. Sabbreth, the Orgoth who told him who he was, what he was, who calmed the voices and gave his life purpose again. Sabbreth was who stood beside him now. He hadn’t heard her approach while he was lost in memories that he wasn’t sure were really his. "How can she be back?" he asked, without raising his head. "We climb back on a ladder of bones and souls," Sabbreth replied. "The Reaper Covenant are the ones who ensure our immortality. Just like you, she is the scion of a lineage of great slayers. Her soul must have been marked the moment it slipped free of her body. They brought her back, the same way they will bring you back, if you earn it." "She was so young then," he said. "Do the dead grow older?" "Who understands the dead?" Sabbreth asked. "Was it her?" "She was so different," Orsus began, but then he paused, the words seeming to catch in his throat. "But it was her. What will they do with her?"

name: Name
body:
"She’s one of them now," Sabbreth said. "A great honor. They will train her as a warwitch. Perhaps the other child will be her first sacrifice."
Orsus closed his eyes. He saw the dark-haired little girl, so different from the child he had buried, and yet those eyes were so familiar. In his imagination, she wore the accoutrements of the warwitches and held a curved blade in her small hands.
Bound on a stone before her was the boy he had carried from Umbrey, the child they said was the heir of Vlad Tzepesci. Branka closed her eyes and raised the knife above her head. When she opened them again, those familiar eyes had turned black.
Orsus shook his head slowly.
"You don’t like that?" Sabbreth asked.
"I don’t."
"Then perhaps we can help each other once again."
***
There was very little for the Orgoth soldiers to do outside the ruins of the palace. Aware of the presence and potential scrutiny of the warwitches of the Reaper Covenant, they had initially tried to look busy and industrious, and at first, there had been plenty of work digging pits and erecting temporary fortifications. After a few days, however, most of them were bored and wished that they were on the front lines somewhere far away, fighting against the armies of Immoren.

name: Name
body:
It didn’t help that the vistas surrounding the ruins were not much to look at. If there had ever been a clear day, they would have been able to take in the nearby headlands or look across the waters where the Lothpool drained into the Meredius to the south. But there hadn’t been a clear day since their arrival, smoke and clouds constantly impairing their vision so that all they could see were the ghostly ruins and their own troops.
This made standing watch a largely pointless endeavor, though they did so all the same, day and night. Not that there was much threat of attack. This region had practically been pacified before they even arrived, it had so few inhabitants, and those villages that did dot its length and breadth had already been taken by the Orgoth long before they took up their station at the palace ruins.
The nearest city of note was Skrovenberg, on the far side of the bay, which was held by a larger allotment of Orgoth soldiers. For the time being, the press deeper into Khadoran territory had been arrested by the arrival of the Reaper Covenant and the resulting reorganization of their troops. Hence, an uneasy stalemate currently existed to the east, where the Orgoth held a line near New Vroggen but hadn’t yet pushed farther toward the Khadoran capital, even as the Khadoran forces launched occasional skirmishes but had not yet tried to retake their lost land. They seemed content to use the lull in hostilities to fortify their existing defenses.

name: Name
body:
Fighting was still ongoing to the south, however, where the Immorese kingdom of Ord had largely fallen before forces commanded by Kishtaar, the Howling Silence. That was where most of these soldiers wished they were, wetting their blades with the blood of foes rather than whiling away the hours playing games of chance, cooking meat on spits, or taking their shift on watch to stare fruitlessly into the swirling smoke.
Any commander knows that boredom can be a greater threat than the enemy, and even the Orgoth were not immune to its hazards. It was due to this boredom, as much as the concealing smoke, that it took so long for the alarm to be raised. Soldiers were on watch, but days of inactivity, the unfamiliar cold of the Khadoran winter, and the hazy, filtered late afternoon sun all conspired to lull them.
So it was that it took them several extra moments to register what they saw as the smoky air around them grew slowly brighter, suffused with a warm amber glow, not unlike the engines of their warjacks. By the time the alarm began, the first of the burning wagons had already come careening out of the smoke and smashed itself into flaming splinters against the earthwork barricades.

name: Name
body:
The first wagon was followed by another, and then another, far enough apart that the alarm from the first hadn’t yet spread to the location where the second came blazing out of the smoky afternoon. Even as horns were raised to lips to sound warning notes, the crack of hunting rifles echoed, and an Orgoth soldier fell, clutching at his throat.
Then the ravens descended in a feathered cloud from the smoky sky, drawing fire, pecking at eyes. Shadowy figures loped out of the haze, tall as warjacks, while beasts of prey pounced seemingly from out of nowhere.
Surprise threw the camp temporarily into chaos, but the Orgoth were seasoned and hardened to war in a way that few soldiers in the Iron Kingdoms could match, and the disarray didn’t last long. By the time the last of the flaming wagons had struck the barricades, command had been reestablished, and defensive lines were being set around the palace, with ulkors sent to the front to try to match the ferocity of the monsters that were charging over the Orgoth barricades.

name: Name
body:
That was when the real attack came.
***

name: Name
body: The alarm spread through the camp outside, and Sabbreth grinned at Orsus—to call it a smile would be too generous; a smile was an expression he had never seen on her feral face. "Now is your opportunity," she said and left him standing alone beneath the fading moon. At the end of the day, there were many things that Orsus no longer knew, if he ever had, but there were things that he instinctively understood. Tactics had always come as naturally to him as breathing, and that didn’t end just because he wasn’t standing on the battlefield. He could not yet comprehend the complex and vicious internal politics of the Orgoth, but he knew that Sabbreth had never helped anyone—would never help anyone—if it did not benefit her own plans. She hadn’t explained any of this to him, but he understood it nonetheless. The strike against the child had never been her objective. It had been foisted upon her, and she resented it. Though she would never go against the Reaper Covenant, she had her own machinations, and if their plans for the boy fell apart, then her own goals could only benefit thereby. And by letting him be the instrument of the boy’s escape, the blame would never fall on her.

name: Name
body:
She thought that she was using him as a tool again, as so many had throughout his life. That was fine. It benefited him for her to think that. Though the Orgoth accorded him a kind of respect he had never experienced in the Khadoran military—where grudging acceptance and outright fear had been his lot most of the time—they still believed that he was little more than a weapon, albeit an extremely valuable one.
He knew better. Perhaps he hadn’t, before the moment he saw Branka’s eyes again, but now he remembered. He was not the axe that was chained to his wrist. He was something more than that. They would learn it, too, even if it was the last thing he ever taught them.
"You could be a carver," Lola had told him once, the first time he had said that he wanted to marry her. "A wood-carver. With a shop in the village, making puzzle boxes for Giving Day and the other festivals."
That hadn’t happened, though. Lola had been taken from him. Everything had been taken from him. He had never made puzzle boxes or anything else. All he had ever done, all he had ever been, was murder given human form. For a long time, he had believed that he was doing good work. That he was serving his country, his queen. That he was doing his duty.

name: Name
body: Then, he saw how little all those things mattered in the end. There was no loyalty, no duty, only ashes and the mechanical pieces of a puzzle box that fit together where they needed to go until they were no longer needed. There had been a time when he believed he was a soldier and other times when he believed he was a monster. Now, he was finally content with what he was, but only because he knew that, once upon a time, he had made something. One good thing. He and Lola had made it together. It had been taken from him, too. Held out like a carrot on the end of a stick to make him march, then dashed to pieces when it was no longer useful. Now it was back. The Orgoth had brought it back and, no matter how much they might truly value him—his strength, his tactical acumen, his ruthlessness—they would try to use it against him, too, sooner or later. They would try to manipulate him, as he had always been manipulated—first by Aleksei and the bratyas, then by his country and his queen. He would show them he could no longer be led like an animal on a leash. He was his own man now, for perhaps the first time in his life, and if he fought at the side of the Orgoth—if he dragged himself back from death on a ladder of bones and souls—it would be for himself.

name: Name
body: This life suited him, and he was ready to embrace it. But there was one thing he would not do. He would not let them throw away the one good thing he had ever done. Would not let them sully it, tarnish it, or use it against him. He would die first, or they would. *** Sorscha had sent two squads of hunters along with Lesnoi and his beasts to make the plan work—forces she couldn’t really afford to spare. But it had worked. They had gathered the wagons from abandoned villages along the way, pulled along behind bears that were not happy about the task. They needed to distract the enemy, confuse them, make them think the attack was coming from the front. "There’s a large Orgoth force waiting outside," Lesnoi had reported, the message conveyed to him from his ravens. "Much bigger than ours. A frontal assault won’t accomplish much more than bloodying the ground." "Then we’ll have to try something different," Sorscha had replied. The surprise had worked, sending the Orgoth camp into disarray and focusing their attention on the barricades to the east while the rest of her forces worked their way around to the least likely point of attack—the headlands directly behind the ruins.

name: Name
body:
Here, the Orgoth presence was virtually nonexistent by comparison. The headlands were inhospitable, and there was no good way to reach them except by boat without crossing occupied territory. No Khadoran force, no matter how small, could have slipped through. The Umbreans, however, were woodsmen of almost preternatural skill, more so even than the Kossites Sorscha had fought alongside in the past. For them, maneuvering around the Orgoth encampment in the smoky twilight seemed like second nature.
She had seen the Orgoth fight in the valley, and she knew that the element of surprise wouldn’t last. Therefore, she had to make the most of it. This was a strike-and-withdraw mission, and Lesnoi told her that the target was somewhere inside the ruins themselves, so that was where they struck.
First, the primalists snuffed out the handful of guards who were posted on this side of the encampment, using the noise of the alarm raised by the burning wagons to cover their actions. Then, the time for stealth had passed. Bears weren’t stealthy. Rifles weren’t stealthy. And Drago certainly wasn’t stealthy.

name: Name
body:
So, Sorscha simply let the warjack off its leash and watched as it smashed through the stone walls to get to what it was after.
The reaction was immediate. Orgoth soldiers were there almost as soon as the first wall fell, barbed bolts glancing off Drago’s armor and the shields of the liegemen. The reports of rifles started up as did the deeper coughs of the blunderbusses carried by the bear-riding cavalry.
It was the first time she had seen the Umbrean soldiers fight, and she was impressed with their discipline. She supposed it shouldn’t have surprised her, given that she knew Omirov had been involved in their training, but their wild appearance made her expect something more uncontrolled. Yet they moved like the proverbial well-oiled machine, each piece falling into place precisely when it was needed.
The wardens held the front with shields and axes, matching the viciousness of the Orgoth with ferocity of their own. The primalists tripped up the enemy and defended their forces while the hunters fired and fell back, letting the more heavily armored troops take the brunt of any attack.

name: Name
body:
Each one had their part to play, and all of them were there to keep a channel open so that Sorscha and Drago could get into the ruins—and then get back out. That’s what she had said, anyway, though Sorscha was not at all sure she would ever be coming out again.
At first, the bears made for a formidable force in the midst of the Umbreans, carving a path every bit as effectively as a heavy warjack might have. Then, something Sorscha had never seen before came barreling out of the smoke. It was the size of a warjack, but it was alive, its shaggy body moving with a simian gait as an Orgoth soldier in black armor rode on its back and fired a massive harpoon that speared through one of the bear riders, dragging him from his perch and into the rending arms of the monster.
Sorscha’s first impulse was to pull Drago back to fight the enormous beast, but she couldn’t. She didn’t even have time to see how the encounter played out. She had a more urgent mission, though whether it was the boy or the Butcher, she still couldn’t say.

name: Name
body:
She followed the heavy warjack as it tore through the walls of the ruined palace in search of Vlad’s son, knowing that where it found him, she would find the Butcher. Sorscha had never been to Khazomir’s Palace before but had heard stories. She was surprised to see much of the building still at least partially intact, though the upper floors were gone, and many of the chambers now stood open to the elements.
Here, the volcanic heat from the nearby headlands and the ocean breezes from the Meredius prevented snow from accumulating. Sorscha could imagine vines and weeds running rampant throughout the ruins during the spring and summer.
As she followed Drago, images of what she might find at the end of her journey strobed through her mind. She saw the Butcher, flanked by a trio of the massive, alien warjacks, a vicious smile on his face and that howling axe in his hand. She saw Vlad’s son, laid open on some blasphemous altar, his entrails wound from his body while his still-living eyes pleaded with her to end his suffering.

name: Name
body:
In all the scenarios she manufactured, she never imagined one in which she didn’t encounter the Butcher. Somehow, she knew that he would be waiting for her here. She had never believed in destiny or prophecy, though she had often been caught up in the schemes of those who did, but there was something about this encounter that felt inevitable…or perhaps she simply couldn’t let herself accept the eventuality that all this might come to nothing, neither death nor vengeance but simply anticlimax.
What would be left to her then?
For all the scenarios she envisioned, however, she was unprepared for the one she faced. When Drago smashed down the last wall and stood heaving, like a hunting hound panting from the chase, in an open courtyard, she saw the Butcher not flanked by warjacks, not charging at her, not mocking her feeble attempts at vengeance. She saw him stumbling from a doorway with two small children in tow.
He was smeared with blood and, though she saw several cuts on his face and abdomen, she surmised that most of it wasn’t his own. The axe was still clamped to his right hand, but in his left he held the hand of a little girl who, in turn, held the hand of young Vlad.

name: Name
body:
The presence of the two children should have made the Butcher seem bigger by comparison, but for some reason it did the opposite. He seemed to shrink beside them until he was little more than a child himself.
Drago itched to kill, and Sorscha itched to let it do so, but something was wrong.
Sorscha didn’t know who the little girl was, but she knew she had seen her before. The girl in her dream, the one playing with the blocks in front of the hearth. As the children drew up short in front of the warjack, their eyes met Sorscha’s gaze, and she saw recognition and expectation in them.
The Butcher had been looking behind him but now he, too, turned and saw first Drago and then Sorscha.
"It’s you," he said, before Sorscha could gather her wits enough to speak. "I guess it would be. You came to take him back. That’s good."
Sorscha wanted to dispute his claim, but she couldn’t. It was like the words had frozen inside her. As if all her thoughts and feelings had tried to simultaneously squeeze through an impossibly tiny door. She simply stood, small beside the big warjack.

name: Name
body: "You know me," the Butcher said. "And I should know you, but it’s gone. So many things are gone for me now. But I know that you hate me. These voices, they say that I did something terrible. I do many terrible things." Sorscha’s grip tightened on Frostfang, her knuckles white beneath her gloves. "Take him," the Butcher said, pushing the boy toward her. Then he nudged the girl forward similarly. "Take her, too, or she will be raised as one of the Orgoth." "Who is she?" Sorscha managed to ask, though they were not the words she had expected to be the first she exchanged with this monster in this setting. "She is my daughter," the Butcher replied. "Or she was, once. Now, maybe, she is someone else. But she should be who she is, not who they would make her, who she would be in my shadow." Blood is nothing, Sorscha heard herself telling the young prince. And however you turn out—great or disappointing—will be because of what you do, not because of who your father was. "You know I mean to kill you," Sorscha said, and it wasn’t a question.

name: Name
body:
"I do."
"Then why? Why turn her over to me? Why tell me who she is?"
"You fought for him," the Butcher said, indicating the boy. "Our burdens should not be theirs."
"And you think I can free them?"
The Butcher shrugged his massive shoulders, a strangely human gesture. "I know that I can’t."
For what felt like a long time but couldn’t have been more than a few seconds, they just stood like that, and then Sorscha nodded to the two children. The Butcher let go of the little girl’s hand, and she and the young prince ran behind Drago.
"We could end it here," the Butcher said, after a moment. "I suppose there is probably still a little fight in me, if you want your satisfaction. I don’t think we have long before the Orgoth arrive, though, and then what will happen?"
Sorscha clenched her teeth until she thought they would shatter. She saw the Butcher’s jaw split by the spike of Frostfang, saw him drooling blood onto the ground before he died. She smelled the iron tang of blood on the air as she waded through another village where he had left no one alive in his wake. She felt her father’s hand ruffling her hair before he rode off to battle for the last time, to be cut down by his own commanding officer.

name: Name
body:
A tear streaked down her cheek from her remaining eye, and her shoulders sagged. Her grip on Frostfang loosened such that she almost dropped it to the ground.
"The next time," she said, and though it took all her remaining willpower to do so, she turned her back on her father’s murderer and walked past Drago to where the two children stood. She sheathed Frostfang in the strap on the back of her warcaster armor and took each child’s hand in her own.
"The next time," she heard the Butcher echo, just before she stepped out of the courtyard and left him behind.

name: Name
body:
The little cabin in the Umbrean foothills smells of chamomile flowers. The afternoon sun is golden, and the birds outside sing a song that heralds the approach of spring, but in the shady places under the trees there is still snow on the ground, and when she steps outside in the morning, her breath steams in the air, and the hollow place where her eye used to be still stings with the cold.
Soon, though, even the last lingering snow will melt, and wildflowers will begin to bloom on the hillsides. Frostfang hangs on a hook beside the door, and her warcaster armor hangs in the closet. The strongest thing she’s had to drink in three months is the tea that the so-called daughters of Zevanna Agha bring her.
Today, there is a bite of cold in the air, and so the children play on the floor in front of the hearth, where she has kindled a small fire. Vlad—these days, it only hurts a little to think of him as Vlad—plays with a wooden toy carved in the shape of a warjack, a gift from Omirov. Branka plays with blocks, though now Sorscha can read the letters printed on them.

name: Name
body:
On an afternoon like this, it’s easy to forget that the Orgoth are not so many miles distant. That armies are clashing over the fate not just of Khador but of all Immoren. That the battle will soon be on their doorstep.
Even on an afternoon like this, though, there are reminders. When Sorscha looks out the window, she can see Drago in the shed next to the cabin. The warjack has been quiet since they made their way back from Khazomir’s palace, but not grown still. Sorscha has brought it out almost daily to work with it, keep it in good condition, and strengthen their bond.
The children need no such practice. Both take to the aged warjack like a big, metal brother, and both seem to show the early signs of warcaster potential.
Several of the former soldiers under her command joined up with Omirov’s liegemen. She sees them sometimes when she joins the Umbreans for training. She has a long way to go to get back to her old self—and she has to get used to fighting with one fewer eye. Shooting, in particular, has proven a challenge, but Omirov’s hunters are helping her learn.

name: Name
body:
The other day, Branka asked if they could call her "Auntie Sorscha," and she surprised herself by saying yes. There had been times when she was with Vlad when she had imagined having his child. But even then, it had been more about him than it was about being a mother. She had never really thought of herself as a mother and, honestly, still doesn’t. But she has taken to being an auntie more easily than she would have expected.
Sooner or later, she knows, something will come to their door. Omirov has told her, through the connections he still had to the Khadoran government, that the search for the imperial heir has not waned, even as the Orgoth continue to beat against the Khadoran defenses. Either or both could be here any day. Them, or something else. Something not yet foreseen.
Sorscha isn’t sure what she’ll do when those things arrive. She’s gotten used to taking it one day at a time. For now, she’s just looking forward to spring, when the children will pick wildflowers on the hillside and ask her what they are, and she can tell them that she has no idea.
